clue.text: This queen is one murdered by the French

indicators.note: standing by something means placed right next to it, so the last piece sits beside the one before

parts.note: taken as written
Abel, in Genesis, was murdered by his brother Cain
la is a French word for the

explanation.surface: A queen meets a violent end at the hands of the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Murdered by the French' reads as one event, but it splits: the murdered one is the Bible's first victim, and 'the French' is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Several historical royal consorts bore this name, including the French-born wife of England's Edward II.

clue.text: Simple fellow meets one a/c, a seller of benefices

indicators.note: when one person meets another they come together, so the pieces are joined side by side

parts.note: Simple Simon of the nursery rhyme
the Roman numeral for one
a/c is the abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: A naive man runs into an account, then a corrupt church official selling posts.
explanation.walkthrough: Simony, named after Simon Magus, is the buying or selling of church offices; the nursery-rhyme Simon supplies the letters instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Simony is the sin of trading in church offices, and one who practises it, such as selling livings, is called by this term.

clue.text: Like Pickwick, for 'example, a sight when at rest?

indicators.note: being at rest means lying in a bed, so the sight goes inside the resting place

parts.note: a bed is where one rests
a spectacle is a striking sight

explanation.surface: Dickens's Mr Pickwick, perhaps, makes a curious sight while asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Pickwick, hero of Dickens's Pickwick Papers, is always drawn wearing round spectacles. The stray apostrophe in the clue is a printing slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Pickwick is famously pictured wearing glasses, and a person who wears glasses is described with this adjective.

clue.text: "On the Beach" as written for the listener

indicators.note: something meant for a listener is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: literal means exactly as written, word for word

explanation.surface: Reading out the title of the novel On the Beach exactly as it is printed.
explanation.walkthrough: On the Beach is a Nevil Shute novel, but here the phrase is just a definition: the shore zone.
explanation.definitionFit: This adjective and noun refer to the shore region, the strip of land along a sea or lake coast.

clue.text: Drink prepared in baths

indicators.note: a dish that is prepared is made up from its ingredients, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A drink mixed up in bathtubs, like bathtub gin.
explanation.definitionFit: This green, wormwood-flavoured spirit is a strong alcoholic beverage, once banned in France.

clue.text: Doctor introduces musical yarn

indicators.note: one who introduces something comes before it, so the first piece leads the second

parts.note: MO is Medical Officer, an army doctor
Hair is the 1960s rock musical

explanation.surface: A doctor introduces a story that is musical, or launches a show.
explanation.walkthrough: Yarn looks like a tall story, but it is the wool.
explanation.definitionFit: This fabric thread is spun from the hair of the Angora goat and used for knitting and weaving.

clue.text: Car taking road to the six counties

indicators.note: to here means heading up to, so the first piece runs on into the second

parts.note: the M1, Britain's first motorway, written with I for 1
Northern Ireland is made up of six counties; NI is its abbreviation

explanation.surface: A car being driven along the road to Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is a major English motorway; crossword setters often write its 1 as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: The small British car launched in 1959 became an icon of the Sixties and still carries the name.

clue.text: Turned extremely hazy, perhaps, with rumblings of a storm

indicators.note: perhaps hints at one possible version of the letters, so they may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of hazy

explanation.surface: The weather turned close and hazy, with a storm grumbling in the distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; the signal is 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Weather marked by the low growl and crash of approaching storms is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Fine bass first caught in mistake for puffer

indicators.note: something caught in a net is held inside it, so these letters go within another word

parts.note: bish is British slang for a blunder

indicators.note: first tells us which of the two pieces goes ahead of the other when they are joined

parts.note: a bass voice or note is a low one
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads

explanation.surface: A good bass, caught first, is wrongly taken for a pufferfish.
explanation.walkthrough: Fine bass reads as an angler's prize; bass is the low voice, and bish is dated British slang for a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: The puffer is a fish that inflates itself when threatened, and this is its other common name.

clue.text: A pharmacist's current measuring units

parts.note: taken as written
MPS, Member of the Pharmaceutical Society, a qualified pharmacist; the 's joins it on

explanation.surface: A chemist's units for measuring electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrical current is measured in amperes, and this short form is the everyday name for those units.

clue.text: The state of being terrified of Medusa?

definitions.text: The state of being terrified of Medusa?

parts.note: surface reading: being scared stiff
setter's reading: the Gorgon Medusa turned anyone who looked at her into stone

explanation.walkthrough: Petrified means both terrified and turned to stone; Medusa, the Gorgon of Greek myth, did the latter to those who met her gaze.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the process or condition of being turned into stone, which is what Medusa's gaze did to her victims.

clue.text: Apt development before many send off for hi-fi equipment

indicators.note: a development is a change in form, so the letters of the word before it are reshaped

parts.note: the letters rearranged
ere is an old word for before
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a large number
to order goods is to send off for them

explanation.surface: A fitting move before many people write away for stereo gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like a joining word but supplies a piece of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This machine records and plays back sound on magnetic tape and was a staple of home stereo systems.

clue.text: One treading delicately in the kitchen

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a person who walks with short, dainty steps

definitions.note: the One of the clue does double duty: one found in the kitchen
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a machine that chops meat finely

explanation.surface: Someone tiptoeing about the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: To mince is to walk with affected little steps, and also to chop food into tiny pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names both someone who walks affectedly with dainty steps and a grinding appliance that chops meat finely.

clue.text: Change of course originally prompting president to create US motorway

parts.note: a turn is a change of direction

indicators.note: originally points to how a word begins, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of prompting
Ike was the nickname of President Dwight Eisenhower

explanation.surface: A change of route, urged by the President, leads to a new American highway.
explanation.walkthrough: Eisenhower, fittingly, created the US interstate highway system.
explanation.definitionFit: In the United States this is a toll expressway, the counterpart of a British motorway.

clue.text: Head of School behaves obsequiously, but puts down bad characters

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top, its opening letter, which is the only one kept

parts.note: the first letter of School
to crawl is to fawn or toady

explanation.surface: A headmaster fawns on others but runs down the troublemakers.
explanation.walkthrough: Puts down bad characters looks like disciplining rogues, but the characters are written letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To write untidy, badly formed letters hastily is this verb, so the characters set down are poorly shaped.

clue.text: Annoyed about unknown Scotsman climbing tree

indicators.note: about here means around, so one word wraps the others

parts.note: sore is informal for annoyed
y is an algebraic unknown

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means going upwards, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Mac is a familiar name for a Scotsman

explanation.surface: An irritated Scot of unknown name is up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbing tree' looks like it all belongs together, but 'climbing' acts on the Scotsman, and tree is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a large maple species common in Britain, known for its winged seeds that spin as they fall.

clue.text: Dark horse on the right coming into bend

indicators.note: coming into a place means entering it, so these letters go inside another word

parts.note: to sway is to bend to and fro

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing on another comes after it, so the first piece follows the second

parts.note: RT is an abbreviation for right
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: An unexpected outsider of a horse comes into the bend on the right-hand side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark horse' reads as one racing phrase, but it splits: 'Dark' is the definition and 'horse' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a dusky or dark complexion, so it is a fair synonym for dark in appearance.

clue.text: Desire simply in a lecherous way

parts.note: to want is to desire
only means merely or simply

explanation.surface: Plain lust, behaving like a lecher.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanton means sexually unrestrained or lewd, and the adverb describes acting with such lustful abandon.

clue.text: Unnecessary to change the Head for being negligent'

indicators.note: changing the head means swapping out the top letter, replacing it with the one named

parts.note: needless means unnecessary
H is an abbreviation for head, used on pencils and in sport

explanation.surface: No need to replace the headteacher just for being careless.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter of the word for unnecessary is swapped for H. The stray apostrophe at the end is a printing slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pays no attention to warnings or duties is careless, which is what being negligent amounts to.

clue.text: Funny man accepting arts award? It means just the opposite

indicators.note: something funny is odd or peculiar, so the letters of the next word come out oddly arranged
one who accepts something takes it in, so one word holds the other inside

parts.note: the letters rearranged
a Tony is an American theatre award

explanation.surface: A comedian picks up a theatre prize, which is the reverse of what you would expect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny man' reads as a comedian, but 'Funny' only signals that man is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A word whose meaning is the reverse of another's, like hot against cold, is exactly this.

clue.text: Vessel, say, named by a short fellow?

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the words, so the answer matches their sound, not their spelling

parts.note: named is called, and Ron is a short form of the name Ronald

explanation.surface: A small man gives a name to a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Short fellow suggests someone small, but it means a man's name in shortened form.
explanation.definitionFit: A large metal cooking pot, the kind witches stir, is a container or vessel.

clue.text: Another drink, perhaps? Good reason for abandoning the game
A pound found in an undergarment

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for one pound sterling

definitions.note: a cryptic second meaning: the word is found inside the name of a pair of women's underpants
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the word sits inside the British name for women's underpants, missing only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone discovers a pound coin tucked in their underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Knickers are British women's underpants, and the slang word for a pound sits inside that word.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a single pound sterling is called this, plural unchanged, much as a quid is.

clue.text: The princess's single attendant is a tart

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an unmarried lady attending a queen or princess
second meaning: a small pastry filled with almond curd

explanation.surface: A slur on a royal lady-in-waiting's morals.
explanation.walkthrough: Tart is not a slur on the attendant: it is the Richmond pastry of that name, a small almond cheesecake.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is given both to an unwed noblewoman serving a royal lady and to a traditional English almond pastry.

clue.text: Trendy way to identify the present month

parts.note: in means fashionable
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A fashionable way of telling which month it is.
explanation.walkthrough: In old business letters 'the 5th inst.' meant the fifth of this month; inst. is short for instant.
explanation.definitionFit: This abbreviation, from the Latin instante mense, was used in commercial letters to refer to the current calendar month.

clue.text: Contest appropriate to a politician

parts.note: due to someone means fitting or owed to them
L is the abbreviation for a Liberal

explanation.surface: A fight fit for a politician.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal fight between two people, traditionally with pistols or swords, is a contest of arms.

clue.text: Mischievous associate of some old servicemen

parts.note: the RASC, Royal Army Service Corps, was a British army unit until 1965
an ally is a partner or associate

explanation.surface: A roguish friend of a few old soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Associate' comes first in the clue but its letters go last.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a cheeky rogue, so behaving like one is naughty, playfully troublesome.

clue.text: Local VIP's confusion about opera opening in Scottish port

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

parts.note: a mess is a state of confusion

indicators.note: about here means around, so one word encloses the rest

parts.note: Ayr is a port on Scotland's west coast

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its start, so only its first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of opera

explanation.surface: The mayor's mix-up over the opera premiere in a Scottish harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition keeps its 's: the clue reads 'the mayoress is confusion about...'.
explanation.definitionFit: The woman mayor, or a mayor's wife acting as consort, is a prominent figure in town civic life.
